## Turn structure and the deterministic engine

Each turn is one season, resolved by a deterministic engine from a single seed: the same seed and the same orders always produce the same game. That makes games replayable, debuggable and fair to compare across models.

1. **Income and upkeep.** Provinces pay gold into each treasury; units and employed characters at court are paid, while those away build up back pay, paid on their return. Unpaid characters may leave or turn. From item 11a, characters are hired for jobs with a fee instead of wages, and nothing builds up ("Jobs, not wages").
2. **Arrivals.** Envoys, spies' reports, gold shipments and rumors scheduled for this turn arrive. Each seat sees only what reached it.
3. **Correspondence.** Envoys present at a court hold audiences with that leader. Leaders write instructions, seal tablets and dispatch envoys; travel time is set by distance on the map.
4. **Orders.** Every seat submits secret, simultaneous orders: moves, supports, transfers, hires, checks, spy missions.
5. **Resolution.** The engine resolves combat, transfers, captures, detentions and forgery checks.
6. **World events.** Seeded catastrophes strike; only the affected power learns their full extent.
7. **Reports.** Each seat receives its own view: map, treasury, arrivals, and what its characters chose to tell it.

**What the engine owns.** Positions, gold, units, characters' hidden traits and facts, who knows which fact, travel times, the seed, the end of the game. Nothing in this list is ever decided by a language model.

**What language models own.** Leaders' decisions and letters, envoys' words and choices, the narrator's phrasing. Every model output that changes state becomes an order the engine validates.

**Pacing: sleeping seats and standing orders.** Longer histories, up to the roughly 30 years the letters span, become affordable if model calls scale with events, not with time. The world still advances season by season, but each seat sleeps until something concerns it.

- **Per-seat sleep, never a global skip.** Announcing "nothing happens, skipping three seasons" would tell everyone no armies are moving. Each seat sees only its own wake-ups. Sleep is for model and file seats; script and human seats play every season.
- **Default wake triggers set by the engine.** An envoy arrives, with whatever tablet, offer or audience awaits an answer; foreign troops enter or attack its land or troops, or arrive next to its homeland or a walled city it holds; a siege of a city of its own begins, or is about to make it surrender; it loses land or troops; a scheduled or standing order is foiled by others; a servant gives notice; a ransom is demanded. A report coming home, foreign troops next to its other land and a catastrophe that costs it no troops go to the digest (as built in the fix pass after item 4 and the siege package).
- **A digest for the rest.** Distant troop movements, rumors and market changes are collected and shown at the next wake-up instead of waking the seat. From item 6b, a light alert is first read by the cheaper model, which may wake the seat's own model if it matters ("Light alerts go to the cheaper model too"); what it judges needs nothing goes to the digest.
- **No triggers of the seat's own** (dropped 19 October 2026). Seat-defined triggers ("wake me if Babylon's army leaves Babylon"), the five a seat could set, and the option to raise or lower a default trigger's priority are removed. Each is a way for a king to wake himself, which the simulations showed he will use every season, and none matches what a king could know: he does not learn that his army has reached a place until someone tells him.
- **Scheduled, conditional orders.** "In season 14, move these armies from Kadesh to Qatna, unless Hatti has moved troops into Kizzuwatna." Conditions use a structured, engine-checkable vocabulary (unit at province, treasury below, envoy returned, tablet sealed), never free text. Conditions and targets read only what is known where the order runs (decided 21 October 2026): the stock or treasury there, a fixed amount, or the last report a courier brought, never a fact the engine knows and the sender could not; once item 13 adds distance inside the realm, this holds for every scheduled and conditional order. The same vocabulary serves the conditions of contracts ("If-clauses in contracts"). Orders are re-validated when they execute; a failed order wakes the seat.
- **A safety cap** on sleep, so no seat disappears by accident; it is hidden from the kings (see "The cap is a hidden safety net" below).

The pattern follows play-by-mail games and Kriegsspiel, and the history itself: kings with slow messengers had to give orders in advance and live with them.

**Decided: sleep is the default** (18 October 2026). In the first agent simulation no seat slept: the kings understood the option and never chose it, because sleeping gains a king nothing and costs it attention. So a seat no longer asks to sleep. After giving orders it sleeps automatically until a wake trigger fires or the cap is reached, and its scheduled orders run in between. A king never chooses when he wakes: only the default triggers wake him, events the engine itself judges to concern him, with the hidden cap as the backstop ("No triggers of the seat's own"). Both agent simulations showed why: given a way to wake himself, a king uses it every season (in the second, kings named the very next season in 114 of 130 replies, and sleep saved 6 of 136 orders calls). What he is told is under "What the kings are told".

- **Wake triggers set the cost.** Every arriving envoy, and every foreign army or fleet that enters a seat's land or arrives next to its homeland, wakes a seat, so in a busy season a seat is called anyway, as it should be. The quiet seasons are the saving. The triggers are tuned from the next games' wake-up data, and the digest carries everything that does not need a decision.
- **The switch stays** for experiments, so default sleep can be compared with seats called every season.

**What the kings are told.** The rulebook makes sleep the frame of every decision, not a footnote: "After you give your orders, you sleep. Only these wake you, because they concern you: an envoy at your door; foreign troops entering or attacking your land or your troops, or arriving next to your homeland or a walled city you hold; a siege of a city of yours begun, or about to make it surrender; land or troops lost; a scheduled or standing order that others foiled; a servant giving notice; a ransom demanded. You cannot ask to be woken, at a season you name or for anything else. If none of these happens, you sleep on: you may sleep for the rest of the game. So plan as if these orders must carry your kingdom until it ends: schedule what your armies should do in the seasons ahead, give standing orders for the attacks you fear, and leave your envoys mandates that stand on their own." Each request also tells the king how long it slept and why it woke, so it learns how long its plans had to hold.

**The cap is a hidden safety net.** In principle no ceiling is needed, since a king should plan for the whole game. In practice a model will not, and the triggers will wake it long before. So the cap stays as a fallback only, raised from 6 seasons to 12 and not mentioned in the rulebook, so it does not anchor the kings' planning horizon. Scheduled orders get no horizon tied to the cap: they may run as far ahead as the king plans, and units with no orders hold.

**Envoys who wait.** In the replay of the first simulation under the new triggers, almost all remaining wake-ups came from envoys waiting to be received; routine envoys are to be answered by a cheaper model playing the king (item 6b; "Routine audiences are answered by a cheaper model"). Envoys historically waited at court for months, and Kadashman-Enlil complained his messenger was kept six years, so waiting is in period.

- **Waiting is a tool as well as a cost.** Keeping an envoy waiting can be a slight or leverage, as Tushratta held Mane; a king may choose to let a matter wait even when he could answer at once.

**Dropped: the minister and the attention limit** (19 October 2026). An official who receives envoys in a sleeping king's name, and a limit on how often a king holds court, were considered and dropped. They would only ever act for model seats, since human and script seats play every season, and the game adds no position that exists for one kind of seat only. Every king receives every envoy himself.

**What the replay showed** (18 October 2026). Replaying both seed-7 games: a yearly court saved almost nothing, because nearly every envoy counted as pressing, and what saves calls is answering an envoy without an orders call (an audience costs about 16k tokens, an orders call about 37.5k). Three conclusions:

- **An envoy wakes a king for an audience only.** A king sleeps while nothing changes, and when something happens he is the judge of whether it alters his plan. The audience call gives him a compact picture of his realm (his troops, foreign troops at or inside his borders, his treasury, his scheduled orders, his envoys at court); in it he answers the envoy, may dispatch envoys with letters, tablets and gifts, and either lets his orders stand or reopens them, which runs the full orders call that season. The order triggers (foreign troops entering or attacking his land or troops, or arriving next to his homeland or a walled city he holds; a siege begun or near surrender; land or troops lost; a scheduled or standing order foiled; a servant's notice; a ransom demanded; the cap) still reopen orders directly. The second agent simulation found kings reopening their orders at 3 of the 4 courts held while orders stood, at under 2% of their tokens, so reopening stays the king's own choice and needs no fallback.
  - **If kings reopen almost every time, the kind of message decides.** Reopening becomes available only for matters that can plausibly change a plan: a coalition or alliance tablet, evidence of a broken tablet, a ransom demand, a threat or news of war. Greetings, gifts, grievances and peace renewals are answered in the audience alone. The engine reads the kind from what it can see (the tablet's terms, gold, evidence shown, a ransom) and, for spoken words, from a small sorting pass by a cheap model, which labels the audience and errs toward allowing the reopen. This applies to model seats only; script and human seats play every season. A word list will not do: in the replay one flagged 85 of 110 envoys as threats or news of war, because the letters mention armies constantly. This sorts calls, never changes state, so it keeps the rule that text never moves gold or land.
- **Triggers fire on changes, not states.** Troops that arrived at the border last season wake a king; troops that have stood there for a year do not.
- **The yearly court is dropped.** Its purpose was fairness between seats once a minister answered envoys for the king, and the minister has been dropped too ("Dropped: the minister and the attention limit" above), so every king receives every envoy himself.
